clue.text: Would this member be shorter off the aeroplane ?

definitions.text: Would this member be shorter off the aeroplane ?

parts.words: Would this member be shorter off the aeroplane ?
parts.note: read the structural part's name as two words: it is 'more lengthy' when 'on' the plane, so taken off it would be shorter

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about whether some limb shrinks once its owner leaves the plane.
explanation.walkthrough: A longeron is a lengthwise strut of an aircraft fuselage; split it as LONGER ON and the clue's logic follows: off the aeroplane it would be shorter.
explanation.definitionFit: A longeron is a long structural spar running the length of an aircraft body, so it is a member of the aeroplane.

clue.text: No lines as required abroad

parts.note: O, the figure nought, means none
lines of poetry make up verse

explanation.surface: Travelling overseas means no school lines need writing.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in or to a foreign country across the sea is the same as being away abroad.

clue.text: Where those in the swim can't expect privacy

definitions.text: Where those in the swim can't expect privacy

parts.words: Where those in the swim can't expect privacy
parts.note: 'in the swim' is read literally as swimming creatures in a glass container, open to view from every side

explanation.surface: Fashionable people who are in the swim of society live without privacy.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase for this glass container is also the idiom for a place with no privacy.
explanation.definitionFit: A clear glass fish container lets everyone see in, which is why the phrase means a situation under constant public view.

clue.text: The end of Mr Whiskers

parts.note: 'Mr Whiskers' is a pet name for a rodent, and its 'end' is its back part

explanation.surface: The death of a character called Mr Whiskers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End' suggests death; it is the hind end. A rat's-tail is also a thin lock of hair or a plant name.
explanation.definitionFit: The tail is the rear end of a rodent, here the whiskered rodent named in the clue.

clue.text: Poor sense I'm making of retributive justice

indicators.note: the letters of the words are poorly put together and must be set in a better order

explanation.surface: Bad judgment makes for a kind of payback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' signals an anagram of SENSE IM; 'making of' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Nemesis, named after the Greek goddess of vengeance, means deserved punishment that catches up with wrongdoers.

clue.text: Let it stand without record of seven in play

indicators.note: the proofreading word goes outside, around the record

parts.note: stet is the proofreader's Latin instruction meaning let it stand
EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: A note to leave something unchanged, with no record of seven people in a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' means outside: STET surrounds EP.
explanation.definitionFit: A septet is a group of seven performers, so it is seven musicians playing together.

clue.text: A case of the tuition being incomplete

indicators.note: the letters come from inside the words, neither of which appears complete

explanation.surface: An instance where someone's schooling was left unfinished.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits inside thE TUItion.
explanation.definitionFit: An etui is a small ornamental case for needles or cosmetics.

clue.text: Edgy fellow, might lose his head as a skater

definitions.text: Edgy fellow, might lose his head as a skater

parts.words: Edgy fellow, might lose his head as a skater
parts.note: a man who goes to the brink is edgy; drop his first letter and he becomes a man of the ice rink

explanation.surface: A nervous man could panic while skating.
explanation.walkthrough: Brinkmanship is pushing a dispute to the edge. Without its head B the word leaves RINKMAN, a skater.
explanation.definitionFit: A brinkman practises brinkmanship, pushing a confrontation to the very edge of disaster, so he lives on the edge.

clue.text: One is willing to appoint him

definitions.text: One is willing to appoint him

parts.words: One is willing to appoint him
parts.note: 'willing' is read as 'making a will': a testator names the person who will carry out its terms

explanation.surface: An eager employer is ready to hire a particular man.
explanation.definitionFit: A testator drawing up a will names the official who administers the estate after death.

clue.text: John Hornblower

parts.note: the Cumbrian huntsman of the song 'D'ye ken John ...', who woke the county with his horn in the morning

explanation.surface: Someone named John who plays the horn.
explanation.walkthrough: The song 'D'ye ken John Peel' celebrates a real Lake District huntsman, famous for his hunting horn 'in the morning'.
explanation.definitionFit: The huntsman of the old folk song is remembered for sounding his hunting horn, so he is a John who blew a horn.

clue.text: The essayist had one upon 18

parts.note: Charles Lamb, writing as Elia, produced a famous comic essay whose title opens with this word, on the subject of 18-down

explanation.surface: A writer of essays produced one about a certain subject.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Lamb's 'A Dissertation upon Roast Pig' is one of the Essays of Elia; 18-down gives the rest of the title.
explanation.definitionFit: A dissertation is a long formal essay or discourse on a subject, which is what Lamb's title calls his piece.

clue.text: Vocalists linked with unrequited love ?

parts.note: to 'carry a torch' for someone is to love them without return, and songs of that kind have their own performers

explanation.surface: Singers known for songs of love not returned.
explanation.walkthrough: A torch song is a sentimental ballad of unreturned love, from the idiom 'carry a torch for'.
explanation.definitionFit: Torch songs are laments about unreturned love, and the performers who specialise in them take the name.

clue.text: Gray's favourite ending in a 3

parts.note: Thomas Gray's ode mourns a favourite cat drowned in a tub of gold fishes; 3-down names that container

explanation.surface: Someone called Gray has a preferred thing that finishes in some numbered item.
explanation.walkthrough: Gray's 'Ode on the Death of a Favourite Cat, Drowned in a Tub of Gold Fishes' (1748) is about Horace Walpole's tabby, Selima; 'ending' means her death.
explanation.definitionFit: Selima was the pet cat of Horace Walpole commemorated in Gray's poem, so she is Gray's 'favourite' who met her end in a fish tub.

clue.text: No metric change — that's somewhat phoney

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are to be changed into a new order

explanation.surface: Refusing to go metric is a bit of a sham.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' asks for the letters of NO METRIC to be rearranged; 'phoney' is read as 'like a telephone', not 'fake'.
explanation.definitionFit: An internal telephone link between rooms works much like a phone, so it is a phone-like device.

clue.text: Did it pave the way for Poplar station ?

parts.note: asp is an old name for the aspen, a kind of poplar tree
a halt is a small railway stopping place

explanation.surface: Was this road surface laid for a station in Poplar, an area of East London?
explanation.walkthrough: Poplar is a district of East London, which makes it read as a place name; here it is the tree. A halt is a minor British railway stop.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarmac-like bitumen surfacing is spread on roads, so it literally paves the way.

clue.text: With which sports writers can make quite a splash

definitions.text: With which sports writers can make quite a splash

parts.words: With which sports writers can make quite a splash
parts.note: 'make a splash' is read literally: water sports involve real splashing

explanation.surface: Sports journalists can make a big impression with a certain story.
explanation.definitionFit: Water sports such as swimming and diving are literally splashy events for journalists to report.

clue.text: Its message is mainly for those in obscurity

definitions.text: Its message is mainly for those in obscurity

parts.words: Its message is mainly for those in obscurity
parts.note: 'mainly' is read as 'on the main', at sea, and 'obscurity' as poor visibility in mist

explanation.surface: Some communication is intended chiefly for people nobody has heard of.
explanation.definitionFit: A loud horn on a lighthouse or ship warns vessels at sea when mist hides them, so its signal is for sailors who cannot see.

clue.text: Camford's counterpart ?

parts.note: Camford blends the names of England's two oldest universities one way round; the matching blend takes them the other way

explanation.surface: Asking what matches a place called Camford.
explanation.walkthrough: Camford (Cam- from Cambridge plus -ford from Oxford) is the fictional university in Thackeray and Conan Doyle; the other blend takes Ox- first.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are blends of Oxford and Cambridge used for the two ancient universities together, so each is the other's counterpart.

clue.text: Lamb's meat

parts.note: Lamb is Charles Lamb the essayist, whose famous essay celebrates a dish of pork

explanation.surface: Meat from a young sheep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lamb's meat' looks like mutton; Charles Lamb wrote 'A Dissertation upon Roast Pig', as 11-across notes.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Lamb's best-known essay is in praise of cooked pork, so that dish is his meat.

clue.text: Closed like the ranks of eastern riders, perhaps

indicators.note: the letters might perhaps be arranged otherwise, so they are reshuffled

explanation.surface: Tightly packed, like the lines of horsemen from the East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' asks for E and RIDERS to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Serried means pressed close together in rows, the standard description of tight military lines.

clue.text: Ring up uncle without having to break connexion

indicators.note: the word uncle sits outside, surrounding the other pieces

parts.note: a ring is round, the shape of the letter O

explanation.surface: A phone call to a relative made without being forced to cut ties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' is the old sense 'outside': UNCLE goes round O and UP. 'Connexion' is an older British spelling of connection.
explanation.definitionFit: To detach two linked railway wagons or parts is to sever the link between them.

clue.text: French dialect gives one a spot of trouble

definitions.text: French dialect gives one a spot of trouble

parts.words: French dialect gives one a spot of trouble
parts.note: a regional French speech is hard for a visitor to follow, so it can cause some difficulty

explanation.surface: A regional way of speaking in France causes someone a little bother.
explanation.definitionFit: Patois is the local, non-standard speech of a region, a term borrowed from French for a rustic dialect.

clue.text: Marriage lines one boy returned

parts.note: BR stands for British Rail, the old railway lines
the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: the word for a boy is turned round and read backwards

parts.note: a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: Wedding paperwork concerning a single lad who has come home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marriage lines' is British slang for a marriage certificate, but the phrase splits: BR (British Rail) is 'lines'. 'returned' turns LAD into DAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as a noun, an old word for a wedding feast or ceremony, so it can stand for a marriage.

clue.text: Spirited demonstration of biting the biter for instance?

definitions.meaning: a seance display in which spirits supposedly move or tilt the furniture
reversing the situation on an attacker, as in the phrase about tables and their being turned

explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirited' means involving ghosts, not lively.
explanation.definitionFit: A seance trick with moving furniture, and also the act of reversing one's position against an opponent, the biter bitten.

clue.text: Forbids advance notice of 22, say ?

indicators.note: the word for the wedding notice is spoken and heard as another word

parts.note: banns are the church announcement of an intended wedding, the subject of 22-across

explanation.surface: Asking whether an announcement before the wedding prevents it.
explanation.walkthrough: BANNS, read out in church before a wedding, sounds like BANS.
explanation.definitionFit: Bans as a verb means prohibits, which is what forbids means.

clue.text: Spot the oriental, agent

parts.note: E for east, the Orient
a secret agent is a spy

explanation.surface: Picking out an Eastern secret agent.
explanation.definitionFit: To catch sight of something is to notice or glimpse it.

clue.text: Plot a point against a high church feature

parts.note: a con is an argument against, as in pros and cons
a spire is the tall pointed top of a church tower

explanation.surface: A scheme to argue against some ornament favoured in a High Church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High church' suggests the Anglo-Catholic wing of the Church of England, but here it is just a tall feature on a church.
explanation.definitionFit: To scheme secretly together is to hatch a plot.

clue.text: Horse training began with man's fall?

definitions.text: Horse training began with man's fall?

parts.words: Horse training began with man's fall?
parts.note: after the Fall, Adam and Eve covered themselves, so the era of clothing began

explanation.surface: Teaching horses started when a rider took a tumble.
explanation.walkthrough: In Genesis, after Adam's fall the couple sewed fig leaves to cover themselves: the 'dress age' began.
explanation.definitionFit: Dressage is the training of a horse in precise, obedient movements.
